text: When Black families did try to cross that line and rent or buy on a white block, the answer was often a bomb.
From 1917 through 1919, roughly two dozen Black homes were bombed in Chicago.
Between 1917 and 1920, on average, a Black-owned home or a real estate office that served Black buyers was bombed about once every twenty days.
Almost none of the cases were ever solved, and no one went to prison for them.
The pressure broke open in the summer of 1919.
A Black teenager named Eugene Williams drifted across an invisible line in the water at a Lake Michigan beach.
A white man threw rocks, one struck him, and he drowned.
The police refused to arrest the white man witnesses named.
What followed was a week of rioting.
By the time it ended, 23 Black Chicagoans and 15 white Chicagoans were dead, more than 500 people were injured, and about a thousand Black families had lost their homes to arson.
